The Earth’s velocity for direct detection experiments

Preprint: IPPP/13/95, DCPT/13/190
Christopher McCabe Affiliation: Institute for Particle Physics Phenomenology, Durham University, South Road, Durham, DH1 3LE, United Kingdom
christopher.mccabe@durham.ac.uk
Abstract

The Earth’s velocity relative to the Sun in galactic coordinates is required in the rate calculation for direct detection experiments. We provide a rigorous derivation of this quantity to first order in the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit. We also discuss the effect of the precession of the equinoxes, which has hitherto received little explicit discussion. Comparing with other expressions in the literature, we confirm that the expression of Lee, Lisanti and Safdi is correct, while the expression of Lewin and Smith, the de facto standard expression, contains an error. For calculations of the absolute event rate, the leading order expression is sufficient while for modulation searches, an expression with the eccentricity is required for accurate predictions of the modulation phase.

I Introduction

A convincing body of evidence indicates that there is a large population of particle dark matter in our galaxy [1]. One of the most promising experimental probes of the non-gravitational interactions of dark matter is direct detection experiments. By measuring the nuclear recoil energy spectrum, they aim to reconstruct the mass and interaction cross-section for dark matter to interact with nuclei [2].

For dark matter with local density ρDM\rho_{\rm{DM}}, mass mDMm_{\rm{DM}} and differential scattering cross-section d​σ/d​ERd\sigma/dE_{\rm{R}} to interact with a nucleus of mass mNm_{\rm{N}}, the differential scattering rate (in units of counts/kg/day/keV) is

d​Rd​ER=ρDMmN​mDM​∫vmind3​v​d​σd​ER​v​fdet​(𝐯,t),\frac{dR}{dE_{\rm{R}}}=\frac{\rho_{\rm{DM}}}{m_{\rm{N}}m_{\rm{DM}}}\int_{v_{\rm{min}}}d^{3}v\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{\rm{R}}}vf_{\rm{det}}(\mathbf{v},t)\;, (1)

where v=|𝐯|v=|\mathbf{v}| is the dark matter speed, fdetf_{\rm{det}} the velocity distribution in the rest frame of the detector and vminv_{\rm{min}} is the minimum speed that the dark matter must have in order that a nucleus recoils with energy ERE_{\rm{R}}. The velocity distribution in the detector’s rest frame is simply related to the distribution in the galactic rest frame fgalf_{\rm{gal}} (for which numerous models are known e.g. [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]), through a Galilean boost

fdet​(𝐯,t)=fgal​(𝐯+𝐯Earth​(t)).f_{\rm{det}}(\mathbf{v},t)=f_{\rm{gal}}(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}_{\rm{Earth}}(t))\;. (2)

Here, 𝐯Earth​(t)\mathbf{v}_{\rm{Earth}}(t) is the velocity of the Earth with respect to the galactic rest frame and it is conventionally decomposed into three terms

𝐯Earth​(t)=𝐯LSR+𝐯pec+𝐮E​(t),\mathbf{v}_{\rm{Earth}}(t)=\mathbf{v}_{\rm{LSR}}+\mathbf{v}_{\rm{pec}}+\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t)\;, (3)

the velocity of the local standard of rest (LSR), the peculiar velocity of the Sun with respect to the LSR and the velocity of the Earth around the Sun. These quantities are normally expressed in galactic rectangular coordinates in which XX points towards the galactic centre, YY in the direction of galactic rotation and ZZ normal to the galactic plane in the direction of the galactic North pole. In this case 𝐯LSR=(0,v0,0)\mathbf{v}_{\rm{LSR}}=(0,v_{0},0), where conventionally v0=220v_{0}=220 km/s and 𝐯pec=(11.1±1.2,12.2±2.0,7.3±0.6)\mathbf{v}_{\rm{pec}}=(11.1\pm 1.2,12.2\pm 2.0,7.3\pm 0.6) km/s [10]. Unfortunately there are significant uncertainties on both of these parameters with recent inferences typically finding higher values, see e.g [11, 12]. The impact on experimental exclusion limits due to the uncertainty in v0v_{0} and 𝐯pec\mathbf{v}_{\rm{pec}} has been discussed previously [13].

Given its central importance in evaluating the event rate, it is surprising that there is no rigorous derivation of 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) in the literature. The velocity 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) is especially important for annual modulation searches [14, 15], which are growing in prominence with results from DAMA [16], CoGeNT [17] and CDMS [18], since all of the time dependence in the rate enters through 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t). The de facto standard for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) is the result of Lewin and Smith [19], which includes the first order correction from the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit. In this paper, we provide a rigorous derivation of 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) and we demonstrate that the expression of Lewin and Smith contains an error, as suggested in [20].

In section II we introduce our notation and define the relevant parameters that describe the Earth’s orbit around the Sun. We give two equivalent expressions for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) in section III. Both of these expressions are series expansions to first order in the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit and in the epoch of date, a parameter that accounts for the precession of the equinoxes. The effect of this precession on 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) has not previously been discussed in the literature. Section IV discusses the phenomenological consequences from using different expressions for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) when calculating observable quantities at direct detection experiments. Finally, two appendices contain technical details.

II The Earth’s orbit

The Earth’s orbit around the Sun is described by Kepler’s laws. The purpose of this section is to introduce the parameters that are relevant for our discussion while leaving a more comprehensive discussion to standard texts on the subject e.g. [21].

As shown in fig. 1, the Earth has an elliptical orbit around the Sun. With the Sun at one of the focus points of the ellipse, the Earth-Sun radius is

r=a⁡(1−e2)1+e​cos⁡ν,r=\frac{a(1-e^{2})}{1+e\cos\nu}\;, (4)

where a=1a=1 AU is the length of the orbit’s semi-major axis, e=0.01671e=0.01671 is the eccentricity and ν\nu is the true anomaly, the angle between the Sun-Earth vector and the direction of the perihelion, as shown in fig. 1. The angle ν\nu does not increase uniformly with time, therefore it is conventional to relate it to the mean anomaly gg, which does (gg does not have a direct geometric interpretation but it is related to the eccentric anomaly, which does). There is no closed form expression relating ν\nu and gg but owing to the smallness of ee, a power series in ee is a good approximation [21]

ν=g+2​e​sin⁡g+54​e2​sin⁡2​g+𝒪⁡(e3).\nu=g+2e\sin g+\frac{5}{4}e^{2}\sin 2g+\mathcal{O}(e^{3})\;. (5)

This power series is often call ‘the equation of the centre’.

The numerical values that we quote for these parameters must be with respect to a spatial coordinate system and a reference time. The xx and yy axes of our right-handed spatial coordinate system are shown in fig. 1. We will refer to this as the heliocentric ecliptic rectangular coordinate system since the x−yx-y axes span the ecliptic plane and the Sun is at the origin. The xx-axis points in the direction of the Earth when it is at the vernal equinox Υ\Upsilon, the yy-axis is orthogonal pointing in the direction of the Earth when it is at the (northern hemisphere) summer solstice and the zz-axis points out of the page. This convention differs from some others in the literature in which the xx-axis points towards the autumnal equinox and the yy-axis towards the winter solstice. The reference time from which other times will be referred is the J2000.0 epoch, which refers to 12h (Terrestrial Time) on 1st January 2000. To an excellent approximation, this is the same as noon GMT on 1st January 2000.

The ecliptic longitude ℓ\ell and latitude bb measure the angular distance from the xx-axis and the distance from the x−yx-y plane. The rectangular coordinates of a point on the unit sphere are related to ℓ\ell and bb through (x,y,z)=(cos⁡ℓ​cos⁡b,sin⁡ℓ​cos⁡b,sin⁡b)(x,y,z)=(\cos\ell\cos b,\sin\ell\cos b,\sin b). To an excellent approximation, the Earth’s orbit remains in the ecliptic plane so b=0b=0, while from fig. 1 we see that the ecliptic longitude is related to ν\nu and ϖ\varpi through

ℓ\displaystyle\ell =ϖ+ν\displaystyle=\varpi+\nu (6)
=L+2​e​sin⁡g+54​e2​sin⁡2​g+𝒪⁡(e3),\displaystyle=L+2e\sin g+\frac{5}{4}e^{2}\sin 2g+\mathcal{O}(e^{3})\;, (7)

where L=ϖ+gL=\varpi+g is the mean longitude, ϖ\varpi is the longitude of perihelion and the eccentricity, expressed in degrees is e=0​.∘​9574e=0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}9574.

Following [19], for this work we take parameter values from [22]. They quote

L\displaystyle L =280​.∘​460+0​.∘​9856474​n\displaystyle=280\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}460+0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}9856474\,n (8)
g\displaystyle g =357​.∘​528+0​.∘​9856003​n\displaystyle=357\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}528+0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}9856003\,n (9)

so that

ϖ=282​.∘​932+0​.∘​0000471​n.\varpi=282\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}932+0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}0000471\,n\;. (10)

Here nn is the (fractional) day number from J2000.0. Appendix A describes how to calculate nn given the calendar date. These parameter values are accurate to 1​.′​01\hbox{$.\!\!^{\prime}$}0 between 1950 and 2050 [22].

III The Earth’s velocity around the Sun

We now derive two forms for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t), the Earth’s velocity relative the Sun in galactic coordinates. Although these forms are superficially different, we show that they are equivalent. The first form results from projecting the Earth’s position onto unit vectors that are parallel to the xx and yy axes of the heliocentric ecliptic coordinate system of fig. 1. The position and velocity in galactic coordinates follows when these unit vectors are expressed in galactic coordinates. The second form results from projecting the Earth’s position onto unit vectors parallel to the axes of the galactic coordinate system, whose position is given in terms of ℓ\ell and bb. The components of the Earth’s velocity in galactic coordinates in terms of ℓ\ell and bb follows straightforwardly.

III.1 Projection onto ecliptic axes

The position of the Earth relative to the Sun, expressed in terms of unit vectors ϵ^𝐱\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}} and ϵ^𝐲\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}} that point in the direction of the xx and yy-axes of the heliocentric ecliptic coordinate system shown in fig. 1 is

𝐫=r​cos⁡ℓ​ϵ^𝐱+r​sin⁡ℓ​ϵ^𝐲.\mathbf{r}=r\cos\ell\,\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}}+r\sin\ell\,\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}}\;. (11)

The velocity as a power series follows by differentiating this expression and expanding rr and ℓ\ell in terms of ee. The series can in principle be expanded to any order but in practice, an expansion to first order in ee is sufficient. In that case, the velocity is

𝐮E​(t)=−⟨uE⟩​(sin⁡L+e​sin⁡(2​L−ϖ))​ϵ^𝐱+⟨uE⟩​(cos⁡L+e​cos⁡(2​L−ϖ))​ϵ^𝐲\begin{split}\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t)&=-\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle\left(\sin L+e\sin(2L-\varpi)\right)\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}}\\ &\quad+\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle\left(\cos L+e\cos(2L-\varpi)\right)\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}}\end{split} (12)

with ⟨uE⟩=a​L˙=29.79\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle=a\dot{L}=29.79 km/s. Here we have neglected time derivatives of ϵ^𝐱\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}} and ϵ^𝐲\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}} (|ϵ^˙𝐢/ϵ^𝐢≲10−5|)(|\dot{\hat{\bepsilon}}_{\mathbf{i}}/\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{i}}\lesssim 10^{-5}|) and ignored terms of order ϖ˙/L˙≈5×10−5\dot{\varpi}/\dot{L}\approx 5\times 10^{-5}.

The problem is now reduced to finding expressions for ϵ^𝐱\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}} and ϵ^𝐲\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}} in galactic coordinates. Let −ℛ-\mathcal{R} and ℳ\mathcal{M} be the transformation matrices from heliocentric ecliptic rectangular coordinates to equatorial rectangular coordinates and from equatorial rectangular coordinates at J2000.0 to galactic rectangular coordinates respectively. Then, ϵ^𝐱=−ℳ​𝒫−1​ℛ​𝐱hel-ecl\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}}=-\mathcal{M}\mathcal{P}^{-1}\mathcal{R}\,\mathbf{x}_{\text{hel-ecl}} and ϵ^𝐲=−ℳ​𝒫−1​ℛ​𝐲hel-ecl\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}}=-\mathcal{M}\mathcal{P}^{-1}\mathcal{R}\,\mathbf{y}_{\text{hel-ecl}} with 𝐱hel-ecl=(1,0,0)\mathbf{x}_{\text{hel-ecl}}=(1,0,0) and 𝐲hel-ecl=(0,1,0)\mathbf{y}_{\text{hel-ecl}}=(0,1,0). The elements of these rotation matrices are given in appendix B.

These expressions also include the inverse of the matrix 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The inverse of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the precession matrix that rotates equatorial rectangular coordinates at epoch of date TT to equatorial rectangular coordinates at J2000.0. This is required because ℳ\mathcal{M} relates equatorial and galactic coordinates only at J2000.0. The physical origin of the precession (‘the precession of the equinoxes’) is due to the torque on the Earth from the gravitational interaction with the Moon, Sun and planets [23]. It causes the position of stars and in particular, the right ascension αGP\alpha_{\rm{GP}} and declination δGP\delta_{\rm{GP}} of the north Galactic pole and the longitude lCPl_{\rm{CP}} of the north celestial pole (which enter ℳ\mathcal{M}) to precess in the equatorial coordinate system. The same gravitational torques cause a separate effect called nutation, however we ignore it because it is always sub-dominant compared with the effect of precession [23].

Carrying out the matrix multiplication and expanding ϵ^𝐱\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}} and ϵ^𝐲\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}} to first order in TT, we find that

ϵ^𝐱\displaystyle\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}} =(0.054876−0.4941090.867666)+(−0.024232−0.0026891.546×10−6)​T\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0.054876\\ -0.494109\\ 0.867666\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}-0.024232\\ -0.002689\\ 1.546\times 10^{-6}\end{pmatrix}\,T (13)
ϵ^𝐲\displaystyle\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}} =(0.9938210.1109920.000352)+(0.001316−0.0118510.021267)​T.\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0.993821\\ 0.110992\\ 0.000352\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0.001316\\ -0.011851\\ 0.021267\end{pmatrix}\,T\;. (14)

For practical use, the epoch of date TT is related to the day from J2000.0 through

T=n36525.T=\frac{n}{36525}\;. (15)

III.2 Projection onto galactic axes

For the second form, the position vector of the Earth in galactic coordinates is found by projecting onto the galactic axes XX, YY and ZZ. Expressing the direction of the XX, YY and ZZ in terms of latitude and longitude (bi,ℓi)(b_{i},\ell_{i}), where i=X,Y,Zi=X,Y,Z, the position vector for each component is

𝐫i=rcosbicos(ℓ−ℓi).\mathbf{r}_{i}=r\cos b_{i}\cos(\ell-\ell_{i})\;. (16)

As with eq. (11), the velocity follows by differentiating this equation and expanding rr and ℓ\ell in powers of ee. To first order in ee, the velocity for each component ii is

𝐮E​i​(t)=⟨uE⟩cosbi[sin(L−λi)+esin(2L−λi−ϖ)],\begin{split}\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{E}\,i}(t)&=\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle\cos b_{i}\left[\sin(L-\lambda_{i})\right.\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\left.+e\sin(2L-\lambda_{i}-\varpi)\right]\;,\end{split} (17)

where, for convenience, we define λi≡ℓi+180​°\lambda_{i}\equiv\ell_{i}+180\degree to absorb an overall minus sign that would otherwise be present. As with eq. (11), ⟨uE⟩=a​L˙=29.79\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle=a\dot{L}=29.79 km/s and we have neglected corrections of order ϖ˙/L˙\dot{\varpi}/\dot{L}, λ˙i/λi\dot{\lambda}_{i}/\lambda_{i} and b˙i/bi\dot{b}_{i}/b_{i}, all of which are smaller than ∼10−5\sim 10^{-5}.

To find bib_{i} and ℓi\ell_{i}, we first find the unit vectors that point in the direction of the XX, YY and ZZ axes in heliocentric ecliptic coordinates through the relation 𝐱hel-ecl=−ℛ−1​𝒫​ℳ−1​𝐱gal\mathbf{x}_{\text{hel-ecl}}=-\mathcal{R}^{-1}\mathcal{P}\mathcal{M}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{\rm{gal}} and then make use of the relation 𝐱hel-ecl=(cos⁡ℓ​cos⁡b,sin⁡ℓ​cos⁡b,sin⁡b)\mathbf{x}_{\text{hel-ecl}}=(\cos\ell\cos b,\sin\ell\cos b,\sin b).

Carrying out this procedure and expanding to first order in TT, we find

(bX,λX)\displaystyle(b_{X},\lambda_{X}) =(5​.∘​536,266​.∘​840)+(0​.∘​013,1​.∘​397)​T\displaystyle=(5\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}536,266\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}840)+(0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}013,1\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}397)\,T (18)
(bY,λY)\displaystyle(b_{Y},\lambda_{Y}) =(−59​.∘​574,347​.∘​340)+(0​.∘​002,1​.∘​375)​T\displaystyle=(-59\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}574,347\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}340)+(0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}002,1\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}375)\,T (19)
(bZ,λZ)\displaystyle(b_{Z},\lambda_{Z}) =(−29​.∘​811,180​.∘​023)+(0​.∘​001,1​.∘​404)​T.\displaystyle=(-29\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}811,180\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}023)+(0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}001,1\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}404)\,T. (20)

As we will show in section IV, the time dependence of bib_{i} and ϖ\varpi can be ignored with little loss in accuracy.

III.3 Comparisons

It should be clear from the above derivations that the expressions for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) in eqs. (12) and (17) are equivalent. We make the equivalence explicit by noticing that the components of ϵ^𝐱\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}} and ϵ^𝐲\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}} are related to bib_{i} and λi\lambda_{i} through ϵ^𝐱​i≡−cosbicosλi\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}i}\equiv-\cos b_{i}\cos\lambda_{i} and ϵ^𝐲​i≡−cosbisinλi\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}i}\equiv-\cos b_{i}\sin\lambda_{i}. A numerical resolution of these expressions confirms that this is true.

We now compare our expression with the two other expressions in the literature that are also valid to first order in ee. Firstly, we compare with the expression of Lee, Lisanti and Safdi [20]. In order to compare expressions, we need to introduce new notation that matches theirs: they define λp=ϖ−180​°\lambda_{p}=\varpi-180\degree, g=ω⁡(t−tp)g=\omega(t-t_{p}), where tpt_{p} is the time at perihelion and define the time t1t_{1} when the Earth is at the vernal equinox Υ\Upsilon (ℓ=0​°)(\ell=0\degree). Their unit vectors are also different; they are related to ours by ϵ^𝟏=ϵ^𝐲\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{1}}=\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{y}}, ϵ^𝟐=−ϵ^𝐱\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{2}}=-\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{x}}. To obtain their expression, we need to relate tpt_{p} to t1t_{1}: inverting eq. (5) gives g=ℓ−λp−π+2​e​sin⁡(ℓ−λp)g=\ell-\lambda_{p}-\pi+2e\sin(\ell-\lambda_{p}). Then, tpt_{p} is expressed in terms of t1t_{1} by evaluating this expression at t=t1t=t_{1}, ℓ=0​°\ell=0\degree. From this we find (to first order in ee) that L=ω(t−t1)−2esinλpL=\omega(t-t_{1})-2e\sin\lambda_{p}. Substituting this into eq. (12) and expanding to first order in ee, we obtain

𝐮E​(t)=⟨uE⟩[cosω(t−t1)−2esinλpsinω(t−t1)−ecos(2ω(t−t1)−λp)]ϵ^𝟏+⟨uE⟩[sinω(t−t1)−2esinλpcosω(t−t1)−esin(2ω(t−t1)−λp)]ϵ^𝟐\begin{split}\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{E}}(t)&=\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle[\cos\omega(t-t_{1})-2e\sin\lambda_{p}\sin\omega(t-t_{1})\\ &\qquad\qquad-e\cos\left(2\omega(t-t_{1})-\lambda_{p}\right)]\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{1}}\\ &+\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle[\sin\omega(t-t_{1})-2e\sin\lambda_{p}\cos\omega(t-t_{1})\\ &\qquad\qquad-e\sin\left(2\omega(t-t_{1})-\lambda_{p}\right)]\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{2}}\end{split} (21)

with ⟨uE⟩=a​ω=29.79\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle=a\omega=29.79 km/s. This expression matches the expression in section B.1 of [20]. Furthermore, using T=0.13T=0.13 in eqs. (13) and (14) gives the same numerical values for the unit vectors ϵ^𝟏\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{1}} and ϵ^𝟐\hat{\bepsilon}_{\mathbf{2}} in 2013 as quoted in [20].

Secondly, we compare with the expression in appendix B of Lewin and Smith [19]. This expression is commonly cited in the literature but it was suggested in [20] that it is incorrect. We demonstrate that this is the case. Lewin and Smith retain the full expression for ℓ\ell in the velocity, rather than expanding to first order ee as in eq. (17). Differentiating eq. (16) and expanding only rr, r˙\dot{r} and ℓ˙\dot{\ell} to first order in ee, we obtain

𝐮E​i(t)=⟨uE⟩cosbi[sin(ℓ−λi)−ecos(λi−λ0)],\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{E}\,i}(t)=\langle u_{\rm{E}}\rangle\cos b_{i}\left[\sin(\ell-\lambda_{i})-e\cos(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{0})\right]\;, (22)

where following [19], we have introduced the latitude of the orbit’s minor axis: λ0=ϖ−270​°≈12​.∘​9\lambda_{0}=\varpi-270\degree\approx 12\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}9. Comparing with Lewin and Smith’s expression, we find that the numerical values of the latitude bib_{i} and longitude λi\lambda_{i} are similar, differing by ∼0​.∘​5\sim 0\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}5 (the sign of bib_{i} is opposite because we use a heliocentric system while they use a geocentric system). While the leading order term matches theirs, the first order in ee correction is different: we find that this correction is −cos⁡(λi−λ0)-\cos(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{0}) rather than −sin⁡(ℓ−λ0)-\sin(\ell-\lambda_{0}), as stated in [19].

IV Phenomenological consequences

We now consider the phenomenological consequences of using different expressions for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) when calculating observable quantities at direct detection experiments.

Firstly, we consider the change in the unmodulated event rate. Typically, the consequences of ignoring the TT and ee dependence in eqs. (12) and (17) are very small. For instance, considering the total rate RR at the LUX experiment [24], the percentage change in RR calculated with TT and ee dependence compared to RR calculated without the TT and ee dependence is always less than 0.2%0.2\%. This holds for the full dark matter mass range (few GeV≲mDM≲multi TeV\text{few GeV}\lesssim m_{\rm{DM}}\lesssim\text{multi TeV}), and for different interactions, including standard elastic scattering, momentum dependent scattering [25] and inelastic scattering [26] (see e.g. [27] for further details of these interactions). In comparison, the change in RR when v0v_{0} is varied by 30 km/s is ∼50%\sim 50\% for elastic and momentum dependent scattering (with mχ=10m_{\chi}=10 GeV) and ∼80%\sim 80\% for inelastic dark matter (with mDM=100m_{\rm{DM}}=100 GeV and δ=100\delta=100 keV). Therefore, when considering the unmodulated rate, we conclude that it is always a good approximation to ignore the TT and ee dependence in eqs. (12) and (17) because the change in RR owing to uncertainties in other astrophysical parameters is much greater.

Secondly, we consider the consequences for the modulated event rate. For a differential cross-section d​σ/d​ER∝v−2d\sigma/dE_{\rm{R}}\propto v^{-2}, which is the form assumed by experiments when they set a spin-independent or spin-dependent limit, the Earth’s velocity affects the rate RR through the velocity integral

g⁡(vmin,t)=∫vmind3​v​fgal​(𝐯+𝐯Earth​(t))v,g(v_{\min},t)=\int_{v_{\rm{min}}}d^{3}v\,\frac{f_{\rm{gal}}(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}_{\rm{Earth}}(t))}{v}\;, (23)

where (for elastic scattering)

vmin=mN+mDMmDM​ER2​mN.v_{\rm{min}}=\frac{m_{\rm{N}}+m_{\rm{DM}}}{m_{\rm{DM}}}\sqrt{\frac{E_{\rm{R}}}{2m_{\rm{N}}}}\;. (24)

We assume the ‘Standard Halo Model’ in which fgal​(v)f_{\rm{gal}}(v) is simply an exponential with velocity dispersion 3/2​v0\sqrt{3/2}v_{0} and a hard cut-off at the galactic escape speed (taken as 533 km/s [28]). In this case, g⁡(vmin,t)g(v_{\min},t) has a simple analytic form [29, 13]. We also assume that all of the time dependence in RR arises from 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t), ignoring other sources of time dependence such as gravitational focussing [30].

Table 1 lists the difference in the peak day and the amplitude of the modulated rate between the exact expression for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) and the expressions and approximations listed in the first column. By ‘exact’ expression, we mean that eq. (11) is differentiated numerically with all time dependence retained and rr and ℓ\ell are expanded to third order in ee. The second and third column show the difference (in days) in the peak day Δ​tpeak=tpeakexact−tpeakapprox\Delta t_{\rm{peak}}=t^{\rm{exact}}_{\rm{peak}}-t^{\rm{approx}}_{\rm{peak}} after 1 year and 14 years from J2000.0 respectively. In 2014, the exact expression predicts that the modulation peaks at about 7.45pm GMT on 1st June. The fourth column shows the percentage change in the amplitude Δ​A=100​(Aexact−Aapprox)/Aexact\Delta A=100(A_{\rm{exact}}-A_{\rm{approx}})/A_{\rm{exact}} assuming that ER=3E_{\rm{R}}=3 keV (the threshold of LUX [24] and XENON100 [31]) and mNm_{\rm{N}} is the mass of a xenon nucleus. We calculate Δ​A\Delta A for mDM=10,100m_{\rm{DM}}=10,100 and 1000 GeV, quoting the largest value in Table 1. The values for the other choices of mDMm_{\rm{DM}} typically differ by a factor of a few.

The first two rows of table 1 show that the expansion of 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) to first order in ee and TT in eqs. (12) and (17) is a very good approximation. In these eqs., we have ignored the nn dependence of ϖ\varpi and the TT dependence of bib_{i} in eq. (17) as they are subdominant. In the next three rows, we consider the effect of ignoring the ee and TT dependence in eqs. (12) and (17). The modulation peaks over a day earlier when e=0e=0 but the change in the modulation amplitude remains relatively small. Ignoring the TT dependence leads to a smaller change but over a timescale of decades, the difference in the peak day can become comparable to the effect of ignoring ee. The change in the amplitude remains small. When both terms are ignored, the difference from the exact expression is the linear sum of the individual differences. In the sixth and seventh rows, we show the changes from varying v0v_{0} and 𝐯pec\mathbf{v}_{\rm{pec}} within their experimental error. The change in the peak day is slightly smaller than the effect of ignoring the first order ee correction while the change in the amplitude is significantly larger. In the final row, we compare with the expression of Lewin and Smith. We find that their expression predicts a peak day which is incorrect by 1.5 days (in 2014).

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that expanding 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) to first order in ee and TT leads to results that are very close to the results from the exact expression. When interested in predictions of the peak day of the modulation, we conclude that the ee dependence should be retained because its effect is larger than the effect from other approximations or varying other astrophysical parameters. If interested in changes of the amplitude, the v0v_{0} dependence is by far the most dominant. The TT dependence becomes increasingly important over a timescale of decades from J2000.0.

These results agree with other phenomenological studies in the literature. Green [23] found that the peak day of the modulation signal can change by up to 10 days if an overly simplistic form of 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) is used. Meanwhile, Lee, Lisanti and Safdi [20] demonstrated that an expansion of 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) to first order in ee is required to accurately calculate the amplitude of the leading modes beyond annual modulation.

V Conclusions

The Earth’s velocity relative to the Sun expressed in galactic coordinates, 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t), is crucial in determining the scattering rate at direct detection experiments. Somewhat surprisingly, many non-equivalent expressions for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) are used in the literature. In sections II and III we have provided a rigorous derivation of two separate (but equivalent) forms: in eq. (12) and eq. (17) respectively. These expressions are series expansions to first order in the eccentricity ee and epoch of date TT. The dependence on TT arises from the precession of the equinoxes and has not previously been discussed in the context of 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t).

In section III we compared our result with the two other expressions in the literature that are valid to first order in ee. We found that our expressions are equivalent to the result of Lee, Lisanti and Safdi [20] (after a suitable change of notation) but disagree with the result of Lewin and Smith [19]. The incorrect equation of Lewin and Smith predicts that the peak day of the modulated rate differs by 1.5 days from that calculated with eq. (12) (or equivalently, eq. (17)). The result of Lewin and Smith has been used as the de facto standard (see e.g. [23]).

We considered the phenomenological consequences of using different expressions for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t) in section IV. For the unmodulated rate, we found that varying astrophysical parameters (such as the Sun’s circular speed v0v_{0}) within their uncertainty leads to a much larger change in the calculated rate, compared to the modest change when using the tree-level expression for 𝐮E​(t)\mathbf{u}_{\rm{E}}(t), which ignores ee and TT dependence. In comparison, the ee dependence should be retained for modulation studies that require an accurate prediction of the peak day of the modulated rate. Ignoring the ee dependence leads to a larger change than varying astrophysical parameters within their uncertainty (see table 1). The TT dependence becomes important over a timescale of decades.

Appendix A Calculating the fractional day number

For the zero of our reference time, we take the J2000.0 epoch, which is 12h Terrestrial time (TT) on 1st January 2000. Universal time (UT) or Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) can be used with negligible error. At J2000.0, the fractional day number n=0n=0.

For a calendar date with year YY, month MM (1 for January, 2 for February, etc.) and (fractional) day of the month DD relative to midnight GMT, the fractional day is [32]

n=⌊365.25​Y~⌋+⌊30.61​(M~+1)⌋+D−730563.5,n=\lfloor 365.25\tilde{Y}\rfloor+\lfloor 30.61(\tilde{M}+1)\rfloor+D-730563.5\;, (25)

where the floor function ⌊x⌋\lfloor x\rfloor gives the largest integer less than or equal to xx and

Y~\displaystyle\tilde{Y} ={Y−1if ​M=1​ or ​2Yif ​M>2\displaystyle=\begin{cases}Y-1&\text{if }M=1\text{ or }2\\ Y&\text{if }M>2\end{cases} (26)
M~\displaystyle\tilde{M} ={M+12if ​M=1​ or ​2Mif ​M>2.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}M+12&\text{if }M=1\text{ or }2\\ M&\text{if }M>2\end{cases}\;. (27)

For example, for 6 p.m. GMT on 31st January 2009, Y~=2008\tilde{Y}=2008, M~=13\tilde{M}=13 and D=31.75D=31.75 resulting in n=3318.25n=3318.25.

Appendix B Rotation matrices

In this appendix we give the elements of the rotation matrices used in section III. The axes shown in fig. 1 are the xx and yy-axes of the heliocentric ecliptic rectangular coordinate system. Geocentric ecliptic rectangular coordinates are related to these coordinates through [22]

𝐱geo-ecl.=−𝐱hel-ecl..\mathbf{x}_{\text{geo-ecl.}}=-\mathbf{x}_{\text{hel-ecl.}}\;. (28)

Equatorial rectangular coordinates are related to geocentric ecliptic rectangular coordinates through the relation 𝐱equat.=ℛ​𝐱geo-ecl.\mathbf{x}_{\rm{equat.}}=\mathcal{R}\,\mathbf{x}_{\text{geo-ecl.}}, where [22]

ℛ=(1000cos⁡ϵ−sin⁡ϵ0sin⁡ϵcos⁡ϵ).\mathcal{R}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&\cos\epsilon&-\sin\epsilon\\ 0&\sin\epsilon&\cos\epsilon\end{pmatrix}\;. (29)

Here ϵ=23​.∘​4393−0.0130​T\epsilon=23\hbox{$.\!\!^{\circ}$}4393-0.0130\,T is the obliquity of the ecliptic and TT is the epoch of date.

Galactic rectangular coordinates are related to equatorial rectangular coordinates at J2000.0 through the relation 𝐱gal.=ℳ​𝐱equat.​(J​2000.0)\mathbf{x}_{\rm{gal.}}=\mathcal{M}\,\mathbf{x}_{\rm{equat.}}(\text{J}2000.0), where the elements of ℳ\mathcal{M} are

ℳ11=−sinlCPsinαGP−coslCPcosαGPsinδGPℳ12=sinlCPcosαGP−coslCPsinαGPsinδGPℳ13=coslCPcosδGPℳ21=coslCPsinαGP−sinlCPcosαGPsinδGPℳ22=−coslCPcosαGP−sinlCPsinαGPsinδGPℳ23=sinlCPcosδGPℳ31=cosαGPcosδGPℳ32=sinαGPcosδGPℳ33=sin⁡δGP.\begin{split}\mathcal{M}_{11}&=-\sin l_{\rm{CP}}\sin\alpha_{\rm{GP}}-\cos l_{\rm{CP}}\cos\alpha_{\rm{GP}}\sin\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{12}&=\sin l_{\rm{CP}}\cos\alpha_{\rm{GP}}-\cos l_{\rm{CP}}\sin\alpha_{\rm{GP}}\sin\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{13}&=\cos l_{\rm{CP}}\cos\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{21}&=\cos l_{\rm{CP}}\sin\alpha_{\rm{GP}}-\sin l_{\rm{CP}}\cos\alpha_{\rm{GP}}\sin\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{22}&=-\cos l_{\rm{CP}}\cos\alpha_{\rm{GP}}-\sin l_{\rm{CP}}\sin\alpha_{\rm{GP}}\sin\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{23}&=\sin l_{\rm{CP}}\cos\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{31}&=\cos\alpha_{\rm{GP}}\cos\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{32}&=\sin\alpha_{\rm{GP}}\cos\delta_{\rm{GP}}\\ \mathcal{M}_{33}&=\sin\delta_{\rm{GP}}\;.\end{split} (30)
